beats.narration_text: ECIS extracts financial guidance signals from earnings calls using four readers and a five-dimensional triangulator. The system includes a prediction layer, a guidance revision predictor with six models, and an advanced analytics stack covering dodge detection, competitive positioning, and linguistic depth analysis. Episode 12 added signal decay half-lives, false positive filtering, multi-quarter signal chaining, transcript quality gates, speech act classification, discourse structure analysis, and automated feature engineering. This week: the system learns to doubt itself. Phase 18 calibrates confidence scores so they mean what they claim, detects when a call's own signals contradict each other, explains every prediction in plain English, and flags inputs the models have never seen before.

props.sparkLine: Now it learns to doubt itself.

beats.narration_text: When the system says eighty percent confident, it should be right eighty percent of the time. Platt scaling fits a logistic regression on model outputs versus actual outcomes — independently per signal type — correcting systematic over- or under-confidence. Isotonic regression offers a non-parametric alternative. Both are fitted on held-out data with time-aware splits to prevent lookahead bias. After calibration, the predicted probability curves align with observed accuracy across every decile.

props.sparkLine: Eighty percent should mean eighty percent.

beats.narration_text: Sometimes a single earnings call sends mixed messages — and the system's signals reflect that. Bullish tone paired with rising hedging. High confidence alongside a high dodge score. Offensive competitive language combined with declining specificity. The contradiction detector scans all signals within each call for these conflicts. Each contradiction gets a severity score weighted by signal strength. And contradictions aren't just noise — they're a signal themselves. A call full of contradictions may indicate genuine uncertainty, a mixed outlook.

Every prediction now comes with a reason. SHAP values decompose each forecast into individual feature contributions — which features pushed the prediction up, which pulled it down, and by how much. A natural language module translates those contributions into plain English. Instead of a raw feature vector, the system outputs: "Company A flagged because hedging rose forty percent while CEO-CFO divergence hit a four-quarter high and dodge score exceeded the sector average." The explanation is stored alongside the prediction for audit and review.

Models are reliable on inputs that resemble their training data. When an earnings call looks unlike anything the system has seen — a new CEO's communication style, a crisis call, an unusual transcript structure — the predictions carry hidden risk. Mahalanobis distance measures how far each transcript's feature vector falls from the training distribution. An isolation forest provides a second check. Transcripts flagged as out-of-distribution receive an automatic confidence penalty that scales with severity. Marginal outliers get small adjustments. Extreme outliers get large reductions.

props.sparkLine: It knows when it's out of its depth.

beats.narration_text: Phase 18 added Platt scaling and isotonic regression for confidence calibration, signal contradiction detection with severity scoring and resolution logic, SHAP explainability with natural language explanations, and out-of-distribution detection with automatic confidence reduction. The system doesn't just make predictions anymore. It calibrates how sure it is, flags when its own signals fight each other, explains why it made each call, and knows when it's out of its depth. Episode 13: When Signals Disagree.

Let's recap with Claude. Twelve episodes built a system that produces confident answers. This one makes the confidence itself honest. A probability of eighty percent is now fitted against what actually happened, per signal type, so the number means what it says. When a call's own signals point in opposite directions, that conflict is detected, scored by severity, and treated as information rather than noise. Every prediction carries a decomposition of which features moved it and by how much, written out in a sentence a human can argue with. And when a transcript looks unlike anything in the training data, the system says so and marks its own confidence down.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the test. Take any model you run that outputs a confidence and ask it a simple question: when it says eighty percent, is it right eighty percent of the time? Most teams have never checked. Paste this into Claude and do the calibration part first, because an uncalibrated confidence score is worse than no score at all — people act on it as though it were true.
